For those that may not realize, these distances are easily traversable within the life of a single human - and much much further in fact. We can never perceive anything as going faster than the speed of light, but from your own perspective (or for instance, from those aboard the ship) you can continue to accelerate with no 'speed limit'. The universe 'cheats' to keep things within the speed of light from your perspective such as making time for you start to slow down (1 second for you might be 10 seconds or even 10 years for a relatively at rest observer) and distances themselves will begin to physically contract but the net result is that you get to travel distances far beyond what you could in the lifetime of a single human.

Here some examples of the math are worked out. In particular if we can build a craft capable of accelerating at 1g per second then:

  • In 3.6 years you can travel 4.3 light years.

  • In 6.6 years you can travel 27 light years.

  • In 20 years you can travel 30,000 light years.

  • In 28 years you can travel 2,000,000 light years.

And according to my calculations, 1400 light years at 1g acceleration would take about 14 years. As an interesting aside 7 of those years are spent decelerating. You accelerate as fast as you can for 7 years and then decelerate for 7 years to reach the object at rest.

This is not a theory (in the colloquial sense). The math is used for instance to synchronize GPS satellites with earth. They rely on extremely high precision atomic clocks yet travel fast enough that relativistic effects make their clocks tick, from our perspective, faster than clocks on earth do. If these relativistic effects were not accounted for GPS errors would accumulate to the tune of 10 kilometers a day!

Essentially our universe allows you to press a 'fast forward' button if you yourself meet certain conditions such as traveling sufficiently rapidly or being within the vicinity of a body with a sufficiently large gravitational pull. Some people may not realize the science in the movie Interstellar, for instance, was based on our actual universe. Of course by the time you reach your destination everybody and everything you knew is long since dead. Although in some mind bending 'paradoxes' if humanity later develops an even faster ship you might make it there in 14 years only to find that people born hundreds of years after you left are already there... Gotta love our universe.

This is all fundamental physics that is used in literally everything space oriented today. GPS, probes, etc. As mentioned GPS is literally impossible without compensating for and precise understanding of relativistic effects. One of the earliest 'proofs' was the Hafele-Keating experiment which has been repeated numerous times to ever higher precision. We now have high enough quality instruments that we've even been able to confirm time dilation (or the relative changing of time) at speeds below 36km/h. (non technical article)

It's actually pretty easy to think about if you bring the speed of light way down. I mean I think the only reason people don't consider this so much is that the speed of light is so high that it seems okay for these absurdities to exist once you start approaching it. But the speed of light could just as well be 1 meters a second when suddenly you'd have relativistic 'magic' happening everywhere around you every day.

So imagine the speed of light is 1 meter a second. That means nothing can ever be perceived as moving faster than 1 meter per second. Let's take two people. One is a person who's going to start running and we're going to assume he can run instantly at 10 m/s on the absence of any effects of relativity. He's going to run 10 meters. The other is a person observing this person.

So what happens?

From the perspective of the person running: The runner cannot see 10 meters of distance pass in 1 second since the speed of light dictates that nothing can be perceived as going faster than 1 meter per second. Consequently length itself contracts from his perspective. He's not moving 10m/s, he's moving some large fraction of 1m/s but what was 10 meters is now instead 1 meter.

From the perspective of the person watching the runner: We know that nothing can move faster than 1m/s so we can't have seen the runner go 10 meters in 1 second regardless of length contraction. So time dilation now comes into effect. Time for the observer is passing relatively slower than it is for the runner. From the observer's perspective he will see the runner move close to 1m/s for 10 seconds. And this affects everything. The observer will have effectively aged 10 seconds in the time that the runner aged 1 second.

Relativity, in general terms, is not a complex concept. The reason it took us so long to realize what was happening is simply because this all seems so absurd. A big part of the discovery of relativity was when we realized that the speed of light is the same from all reference frames in large part from the Michelson-Morley experiment in 1887! People were looking for various elaborate mechanisms to try to explain this in terms of a nice intuitive universe. The leap, and ultimately the reality, is that there was no explanation. It was as it seemed even though that is intuitively impossible. Our universe is unfortunately (or perhaps fortunately!) not so nice and intuitive as we once believed.

The whole point here is that nothing in the universe can be perceived to be traveling faster than the speed of light. Yet, there is no universal speed limit. So for an observer back on earth our ship is going to appear to approach the speed of light but then reach a sort of asymptote at the speed of light and never quite exceed it. The reason there is that from an observers perspective the amount of energy necessary to accelerate continues to rapidly increase and approaches infinity at the speed of light. And consequently traveling 1400 light years will take a bit more than 1400 years. However, for those on the ship when they've accelerated to 290,000 m/s velocity (with the speed of light being about 300,000 m/s) they can continue to accelerate via normal newtonian mechanics just as easily as when they were going 30 m/s.

There is a general idea that there is some largescale "Great Filter" preventing civilizations from arising There are two broad ways that intelligent life could be blocked from forming civilizations, early filters and late filters. Early filters are things like planets forming that can have life, life arising, multicellular life arising from single celled life. Late filters are things like nuclear war, large-scale epidemics, nanotech etc. Note that almost all late filters are essentially artificially introduced. Over the last few years, the evidence has become stronger and stronger that astronomical early filters in the sense of planets being rare or life-supporting planets being rare are very weak filters: that is planets are common and while we aren't as certain, it looks like Earth-like planets are also common. This makes it more likely (although by no means certain) that the major filtration is occurring towards the end of civilizations. We need to figure out what those filters are if we are to have a decent chance as surviving as a civilization. For those that may not realize, these distances are easily traversable within the life of a single human - and much much further in fact. We can never perceive anything as going faster than the speed of light, but from your own perspective (or for instance, from those aboard the ship) you can continue to accelerate with no 'speed limit'. The universe 'cheats' to keep things within the speed of light from your perspective such as making time for you start to slow down (1 second for you might be 10 seconds or even 10 years for a relatively at rest observer) and distances themselves will begin to physically contract but the net result is that you get to travel distances far beyond what you could in the lifetime of a single human.

Here some examples of the math are worked out. In particular if we can build a craft capable of accelerating at 1g per second then:

  • In 3.6 years you can travel 4.3 light years.

  • In 6.6 years you can travel 27 light years.

  • In 20 years you can travel 30,000 light years.

  • In 28 years you can travel 2,000,000 light years.

And according to my calculations, 1400 light years at 1g acceleration would take about 14 years. As an interesting aside 7 of those years are spent decelerating. You accelerate as fast as you can for 7 years and then decelerate for 7 years to reach the object at rest.

This is not a theory (in the colloquial sense). The math is used for instance to synchronize GPS satellites with earth. They rely on extremely high precision atomic clocks yet travel fast enough that relativistic effects make their clocks tick, from our perspective, faster than clocks on earth do. If these relativistic effects were not accounted for GPS errors would accumulate to the tune of 10 kilometers a day!

Essentially our universe allows you to press a 'fast forward' button if you yourself meet certain conditions such as traveling sufficiently rapidly or being within the vicinity of a body with a sufficiently large gravitational pull. Some people may not realize the science in the movie Interstellar, for instance, was based on our actual universe. Of course by the time you reach your destination everybody and everything you knew is long since dead. Although in some mind bending 'paradoxes' if humanity later develops an even faster ship you might make it there in 14 years only to find that people born hundreds of years after you left are already there... Gotta love our universe.
